title: Optimal Trading of Microstructure Mean Reversion

p.t: Optimal trading rests on two questions. The first is empirical: how do the mid, the spread, and the order flow actually move at the time scale where trading decisions live? The second is the control problem: given those dynamics, what is the best strategy, and what does it earn? This paper answers the second question inside a model built, piece by piece, from the known answers to the first. At the intraday scale, four dynamics are documented across four decades of microstructure evidence. (i) The mid's moves revert: successive moves are negatively autocorrelated at the finest time scales [20], the fact that the mutually exciting price models of Bacry et al. [7,8], built on Hawkes processes [22], are designed to reproduce; we used the same family for the clustering of large-order flow [31]. (ii) Displacements are transient: a burst of orders pushes the mid away from value, and part of the push reverts as the book replenishes [29,10]. (iii) In liquid large-tick assets the spread is pinned: when the tick is not small relative to the volatility, the spread sits at one tick almost all of the time and opens to two for brief episodes [14,12]. (iv) Beneath the noise, a diffusion: strip the trading noise statistically and what remains behaves as a Brownian semimartingale. The realised-volatility literature models the intraday efficient price this way and validates it on high-frequency data [3,37]. Together the four force the classical reading, from Roll [33] to Hasbrouck [21]: the observed price is the diffusion of (iv) plus a stationary error carrying (i) and (ii). The natural state variable is the gap: the distance between the observed mid and that latent efficient price.

The theory of optimal trading grew around these facts in four threads. (1) Optimal execution (Almgren and Chriss [2]) schedules a large order against the trade-off between impact and risk; (2) optimal market making (Avellaneda and Stoikov [6]) quotes around inventory risk, solved explicitly by Guéant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia [17] and developed into a toolkit by Cartea, Jaimungal and Penalva [11] and Guéant [18]. Guilbaud and Pham [19] bring the tick grid into this thread (the tick-valued spread a Markov chain, the trading in limit and market orders), yet the mid there follows its own exogenous dynamics, pulled by nothing. Throughout this thread, the book is the venue but the price it quotes is modelled as a martingale: the dynamics above enter as friction, not as object. (3) Another thread trades the reversion itself: an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck spread, signal, or reference price, taken as given. Threshold rules are optimal there [36,35,26]; Bertram [9] maximises the long-run rate of the trading cycle through first-passage times, the criterion we adopt; Lipton and López de Prado [27] give closed forms for a single round trip; and, nearest on the making side, Ahuja, Papanicolaou, Ren and Yang [1] quote around a mean-reverting reference price. That thread supplies the control theory we use, threshold optimality and the renewal criterion, and takes the reverting object as given. (4) The closest line builds the book itself around a latent efficient price: moves fire at the boundaries of uncertainty zones [32], the order flow estimates the price [15], the queue-reactive book re-centres its intensities around a reference one [23]. Sfendourakis [34] unifies the family and stabilises the mid around the efficient price; Pulido, Rosenbaum and Sfendourakis [30] solve full-information market making inside uncertainty zones. There the book is the object of study, and the trading solved on it is market making, around inventory risk.

This paper works the seam between threads (3) and (4): a book of the fourth kind, on which the trading problem of the third is solved. Facts (iii) and (iv) are the inputs: we model precisely those liquid assets, and we take the efficient price to be a Brownian martingale, the driftless core of the semimartingale the econometrics finds. Inside that frame we build an order book whose own dynamics produce facts (i) and (ii), and we derive the optimal trading band in closed form. The organising idea is a parity lock: built from the bid, the two-valued spread of (iii) is the parity, the even-or-odd, of the mid on the half-tick grid, so gap and spread collapse to one continuous coordinate plus a parity bit (Section 2). On that coordinate the mid is a pure jump process whose move intensities lean toward the efficient price; under one balanced-response condition on the flow, the gap's reversion, at the book's leaning rate α, is then a theorem: its conditional mean and stationary covariance are exactly those of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Its paths are not: the mid jumps. The efficient price, in turn, is the long-run forecast of the mid, Hasbrouck's permanent component (Section 2). The strategy follows by renewal-reward, with waiting times evaluated on the Gaussian surrogate those exact moments define, the model's central approximation. It costs three errors, δ being the tick: (a) a reward error of proved relative order δ/(θ -ϕ); (b) a frozen tight-book cost, bounded by the occupancy of open books; (c) a timing error of order δ/θ, which we leave heuristic. In the regime δ ≪ θ -ϕ where we work, (a) and (c) are small.

What comes out is a symmetric no-churn band at the optimal half-width θ * : buy when the gap reaches -θ * , sell at +θ * , hold inside. That half-width solves θ * (θ * -ϕ) = s 2 G (threshold times margin equals the gap's stationary variance) and the band earns rate αs G 2/π e -θ * 2 /2s 2 G . On the surrogate this band is optimal among all admissible strategies, by results from the switching literature; on the jump process itself that reduction remains a conjecture (Section 3). The myopic benchmark (trade as soon as the gap covers the spread) earns exactly zero on the surrogate: the whole rate is the option value of waiting. The band equation is the large-threshold asymptote of an exact first-order condition in the Dawson function, solved in Appendix B, at whose root the rate formula is exact. Simulation places the best band about a fifth inside that root; trading at the root costs three to four percent of rate, at θ * five to six (Section 3.1). Section 4 collects what the solution teaches; proofs and closed forms are in the appendix.

Picture the two prices of the same asset. One is the efficient price X: the fundamental value, real but not displayed anywhere. It moves only on genuine news: on a filtered probability space (Ω, F, (F t ) t≥0 , P) we take it to be an exogenous Brownian martingale, formalised in Definition 2.1 below. This is not a convenience but fact (iv) of the introduction, taken at its driftless core [3,37]; and Hasbrouck's permanent component is a random walk by construction [21]. The other is the mid M : the average of the best bid and best ask actually displayed on the screen, observable, and moved only by the book. Their difference is the gap a stationary error pulled back toward zero [33,20]. The premise here (a modelling stance, not a law of nature) is the existence of the latent martingale X; that the gap it defines is stationary and mean-reverting is a finding in the evidence and a theorem in the model below. Two properties are worth recording now. First, the mid converges to X in conditional expectation: the long-horizon forecast of the mid is today's efficient price, (2.1) Read left to right, (2.1) is the pull: the forecast of where the mid is going lands on value. Read right to left, it is an identification: X is the permanent component of the observed price in the sense of Hasbrouck [21] (stated here, proved as a one-line theorem of the model in Section 2.4), which is what makes the unseen X estimable from quotes. Second, nothing converges pathwise: the limit in (2.1) is taken over the forecast horizon h, not over calendar time; what is stable, stationary rather than convergent, is the distance between the two prices. The phenomenon of this paper is that pull; the question is what trading it is worth. As (2.16) below makes precise, the strategy's profit will not depend on where X goes, only on when the mid strays from it.

p.s: The book, from the bid, and the parity lock
p.t: With tick size δ (the smallest price increment), the displayed bid B t lives on the tick grid, and for a large-tick asset the spread S t takes two values: This is the regime of liquid, large-tick assets, and it is worth saying who lives in it. When the queue at the touch is deep, the spread sits at one tick almost all of the time; a market order that consumes the best queue, or a cancellation that empties it, opens the spread to two ticks for a short while, until a new limit order closes it: the opens and closes of Figure 1, brief by nature [14]. Wider spreads would require emptying two or more price levels before any replenishment arrives; in this class the levels behind the touch are deep and the inside is refilled fast. This is not a claim that any single refilling order profits (adverse selection decides that case by case, and the spread opens precisely when the book has just been hit) but the defining regularity of the class: the tick is large relative to the spread competition would set, so the one-tick spread is worth queueing for, priority at the inside is contested, and spreads of three ticks or more are empirically negligible [14]. We exclude them from the state space. Assets that are illiquid, or whose tick is small relative to their volatility, carry many spread values at once and fall outside the model. Modelling the bid rather than the mid is not cosmetic: the mid is a derived average, and once the spread can open and close, the mid must move in half-ticks. That grid arithmetic has a structural consequence.

p.s: The book, from the bid, and the parity lock
p.t: Fact 1 (The parity lock). Measure the mid in half-ticks, so that it is an integer; parity means whether that integer is even or odd; equivalently, in ticks, whether the mid sits at a half-integer or at an integer. A quote slide moves the mid by two half-ticks, preserving parity; opening or closing the spread moves it by one, flipping parity; and an open is exactly the event that sets S = 2δ. One direction is pure grid arithmetic: Within the two-valued class (2.2) the implication inverts (two spread values, two parities): the spread is the parity of the mid, not a second state variable. What survives is one continuous coordinate, the gap, plus a parity bit that flips at half-tick moves (Figure 1).

Definition 2.1 (Efficient price). The efficient price is the exogenous Brownian martingale with Z a standard Brownian motion and σ X > 0. Nothing in the book enters its dynamics. Definition 2.2 (The book). The book is driven by six counting processes, the moves of Figure 1: slides N s↑ , N s↓ , opens N o↑ , N o↓ , closes N c↑ , N c↓ , each with its own (F t )-intensity. With G t-= M t--X t-, x ± = max(±x, 0), and the spread read off the parity of the mid (Fact 1), (2.5) That λ m is the (F t )-intensity of N m means and no two of the six processes jump at the same time. The mid is then the pure jump process M t = M 0 + δ N s↑ t -N s↓ t (2.7) Throughout, the baselines are positive and the correction is live: µ s , µ o , µ c > 0 and α s , α o ≥ 0, α c > 0. Appendix A.1, (P0), records that a nonexplosive process with these characteristics exists.

None of (2.4)-(2.7) is invented for the occasion. That the event intensities of the best quotes depend on the state of the book is the tradition of Markovian and queue-reactive order-book models: Cont and de Larrard [12] move the quotes at state-dependent rates, and the queue-reactive model of Huang, Lehalle and Rosenbaum [23] re-centres the book around a reference price; both are fitted to exchange tick data, not merely posited. That the moves of a grid-valued price are driven by its distance to a latent efficient price is the model with uncertainty zones of Robert and Rosenbaum [32], where a move fires when X crosses a threshold; and order flow whose intensity is driven by a latent Brownian efficient price is the Cox-process construction of Delattre, Robert and Rosenbaum [15], built there for estimation. Our linear intensities are the smooth analogue of the first and the control-ready version of the second: the minimal specification delivering an exact linear compensator. The same architecture, a book whose event intensities are driven by a latent Brownian efficient price, has since been developed into a unified queue-reactive framework by Sfendourakis [34], with stability of the mid around the efficient price and diffusive limits at the large scale; and Pulido, Rosenbaum and Sfendourakis [30] solve a full-information market-making problem on the uncertainty-zone member of the family, the maker who knows the efficient price steering her quoted volumes. What is new here is not the architecture but what it is made to yield: the parity lock collapses the state to one coordinate, and the position itself, not the quotes, is the control, solved to a formula. The crossing of the mutually exciting models [31,7] is carried here by the gap: a jump up lifts M , hence shifts the balance of intensities against the move: it raises the downward ramp when the gap is positive, releases the upward ramp when the gap is negative, and does both when the gap crosses zero. Just as important, a fundamental that drifts away moves the intensities with it, even while the book stands still. (A transient Hawkes channel with kernel αe -β(

t-s) , as in [31], can be layered on top; it adds short-horizon retracement without changing what follows.) Every intensity is nonnegative by construction. One balanced-response condition equalises the book's corrective drift across parities, 2α s + α o = α c =: α : (2.8) the book responds to the gap, in displacement, however the correction is delivered. This is a genuine restriction, not a normalisation: without it the drift is parity-dependent, -(2α s + α o )G in a tight book and -α c G in an open one, and the single-rate reversion of Proposition 2.1 below would split in two. The condition's bite, however, is bounded by a quantity the tape reports. Why one-sided ramps, and not an exponential kernel. A natural objection to (2.5) is its asymmetry: when the book dislocates, the corrective side intensifies while the opposing side merely sits at its baseline, rather than being suppressed. The choice is forced, and it is worth saying by what. (a) The drift of the gap sees only the difference of the two sides, and for the one-sided ramps that difference is exactly linear everywhere: G + -G -= G identically, so the conditional mean of Proposition 2.1 is exact for all G, not merely near zero. Any pair of kernels with the same difference produces the same drift; what distinguishes them is the sum, the total event rate, which is a variance channel, not a drift channel. (b)

Suppressing the opposing side linearly drives its intensity negative at finite dislocation; truncating at zero restores nonnegativity but kinks the difference, destroying the exact linearity, and forbids wrong-way moves in a dislocated book, which do occur and which the baseline µ of the passive side is there to produce. (c) The level is not a free convenience: one-sided ramps make the total event rate increase with |G|, the two-sided version holds it constant, and the two are distinguishable on a tape: activity clusters when the book is dislocated, which is the queue-reactive regularity [23] carried to the efficient-price setting in [34], and selects the one-sided form. The growing rate also makes silence informative: a quiet book is evidence of a small gap, the channel the filtering continuation of Section 4 uses. (d) An exponential kernel µe βG ∓ agrees with the ramp to first order over the range the process actually samples (|G| of a few s G , itself of the order of the tick), so within that range it adds one curvature parameter the data cannot identify, while destroying the exact conditional mean, the moment identity of Proposition 2.1, and the closed form of Section 3. The linear ramp is the first-order theory of every smooth monotone kernel, and the only member of the family for which the reversion is a theorem rather than an expansion: a one-sided kernel has an exactly linear difference only if it is itself linear.

What the condition costs. Write α tight = 2α s + α o for the tight-book rate and let is of the order of a tick, a ramp with α o > 0 is of the size of its own baseline, and the naive ratio is then out by a factor of several, in either direction, since the ramp on opens pushes p up and the ramp on closes pushes it down. The parity relaxes at rate 2(µ o + µ c ) or faster, and for a liquid large-tick asset closes are fast: priority at the inside is contested, so an open invites the next refill. Whether that refill profits is an adverse-selection question the model does not adjudicate. Thus µ c ≫ µ o stands as the empirical regularity of the class [14,12], and p is small: what has to be small against µ c is the whole numerator of (2.9), baseline and ramp together. Averaging the parity-dependent drift over its occupation gives an effective rate ) so relaxing (2.8) moves the reversion rate by at most p |α c -α tight |. Two readings follow. First, (2.8) buys exactness: with it, Proposition 2.1 holds identically rather than after averaging, and that is what it is for. Second, it does not carry the result. For a liquid large-tick asset the book is tight almost always (p of order one per cent or less), so the split the condition prevents is a correction of that order, and under (2.8) the fitted α is properly read as the parity-weighted rate (2.10), which is the object the trading problem of Section 3 needs. Equation (2.10) is the standard averaging statement for a linear drift modulated by a finite-state chain that is fast against the drift it modulates, here 2(µ o + µ c ) ≫ α, which the same class assumption delivers; we assert it as a bound on what (2.8) excludes, and impose (2.8) in what follows.

The virtue of (2.9) is that p is not a free number to be asserted. It is the fraction of time the displayed spread is two ticks, which a book feed reports directly, and it is simultaneously an output of the specification through µ o /µ c , so the model can be checked against the tape twice over. Figure 2 shows the resulting dynamics in motion.

The central algebra of the paper is one cancellation. Within each pair of intensities in Definition 2.2 the baselines cancel and, since G --G + = -G identically, the kinks cancel too: each pair's net drift is exactly linear in the gap. Weighing each move by its size, ) and the balanced-response condition (2.8) makes the two lines equal: E[dM t | F t-] = -α G t-dt in either parity, exactly. The positive parts exist to keep each intensity nonnegative; they leave no trace in the drift, and the nonlinearity survives only in the total event rate, where the stationary mean defining σ 2 M picks it up. Since X is a martingale, E[dX t | F t-] = 0, and the reversion of the gap follows. We record it together with the stationary structure it forces. The pair (G, S) is Markov (the intensities and the diffusion are functions of the pair alone, and each move updates the spread deterministically by the parity lock) and it is positive Harris recurrent with a unique invariant law π of finite second moment; under π, where σ 2 M is the stationary mean of the book's jump-variance rate m λ m (t)∆ 2 m , with ∆ m the mid displacement of move m: ±δ for slides, ±δ/2 for opens and closes. No dynamics for G is assumed: every identity here is a consequence of (2.5)-(2.8). Proof. The reversion is the one-line cancellation (2.11) closed by (2.8); ergodicity is a Foster-Lyapunov argument with V = G 2 , the Brownian component supplying the required irreducibility; and the moments follow from Itô's formula on G 2 together with the linearity of ( 2.12 4α , both ends explicit in the primitives once p is read off the tape. The two ends meet as the ramps' share of the event rate vanishes, the ratio that also governs (2.9). For the trading problem none of this is needed: Section 3 uses the pair (α, s G ), which the gap's autocovariance (2.14) identifies directly. The forecast property (2.1) promised in Section 2.1 is now a theorem: by (2.13), the fundamental is precisely the permanent component of the observed price. The anatomy respects the causality throughout: between events dG = -σ X dZ, driftless, and the pull is realised entirely at the jumps of M , whose intensities lean toward the fundamental. At an event the gap is kicked by the full move: ±δ for a slide, ±δ/2 for an open or a close, so a tight book kicks by either size, an open book only by the smaller one. We treat G as observable, the full-information case; Section 4 returns to this assumption.

A marketable order pays, relative to the mid, the half-spread which is the only cost in the model, the cost the book itself imposes. Write ϕ t := ϕ(S t ) = S t /2 for its value at time t: a two-valued process, δ/2 in a tight book and δ in an open one. (Any per-lot fee simply adds to it.) One assumption closes the loop with Definition 2.2: the trader is small. Orders fill at the displayed quotes and do not enter the intensities (2.5). Our earlier work models precisely the impact of orders large enough to violate this [31]; the provider's response to being traded against is deferred to Section 4. The strategy is the inventory process q = (q t ) t≥0 . We call it admissible if it is adapted with right-continuous paths, takes values in [-1, +1], and is piecewise constant with a finite expected number of trades on bounded intervals. The cap is a risk limit, and fractional positions are allowed. An independent randomisation drawn at time zero is also allowed; it alters nothing about the book. The trades react to the state the instant it moves (the execution convention below), so q itself is not predictable; the integrands in (2.16) are the left limits q t-, which are. The trader starts flat, and trades are the jumps of q: buys and sells never coincide, so dq t > 0 is a buy, dq t < 0 a sell, and |dq t | lots change hands. Execution is at the touch, a buy paying the ask M t + ϕ t and a sell receiving the bid M t -ϕ t , and we track two markings of the same book: wealth marked to the mid, the desk's convention, and marked to the efficient price, the analyst's:

(2.16) The first reads as a desk reads it: the position rides the mid, and every trade pays the half-spread. The second is the same cash flows with the inventory valued at X: per lot, a buy pays the gap plus the half-spread and a sell collects the gap minus it, and the trade terms are functions of the state alone. The trade term of dW X carries the post-jump gap G t : the trader sees the move and then lifts the quote it left behind. With that convention the two markings differ by W t -W X t = q t G t exactly (Appendix A.5), a difference bounded in L 1 uniformly in t, so the long-run objective below is identical on either; and on W X the inventory term is a zero-mean martingale: q t-is predictable and bounded, X is a square-integrable martingale, so E q t-dX = 0. Every formula in this paper is a statement about the mid-marked book, and the problem is the timing of the gap, not the forecasting of X. The objective is the long-run average profit rate, evaluated conservatively by the lower limit (for an arbitrary strategy the average need not converge; for the band it does, and the lim inf is attained: Proposition 3.1 and Appendix A.7, Step 6) sup q admissible lim inf T →∞ E[W T ] T . (2.17)

One reduction can be dispatched at once: the search over all inventories in [-1, +1], a far larger and harder optimisation, collapses to the three values {-1, 0, +1}, with nothing lost. Unlike the reductions of the next section, this is a pathwise statement about the exact jump process, with no surrogate anywhere in its proof.

For an admissible strategy q = (q t ) t≥0 with values in [-1, +1], define its layers: for each level u ∈ (0, 1], Each layer is an admissible strategy, and, pathwise and at every horizon T , .18) and consequently sup q admissible qt∈[-1,+1] lim inf T →∞ E[W T (q)] T = sup q admissible qt∈{-1,0,+1} lim inf T →∞ E[W T (q)] T . (2.19) The proof (Appendix A.6) is a layer decomposition. The layers at levels u ≤ |q t | hold the full position, with the sign of q t ; the others are flat (a u t = 0); and together they average back to the position, q t = 1 0 a u t du. Gains are linear in the position, so they average exactly across layers; by a coarea identity, so does the proportional cost; and drawing the level at random at time zero gives a single three-valued strategy with the same expected wealth at every horizon, which forces (2.19). The reduction rests on linear reward and proportional cost: under risk aversion or superlinear trading costs, interior positions can be strictly optimal. From here on q takes values in {-1, 0, +1}: a conclusion, not a constraint.

Three further reductions precede the choice of class, and they do not stand on the same footing. The price level is irrelevant information: the pair (G, S) is autonomous (its intensities and diffusion involve the gap and the parity, never the level of M or X), and by (2.16) the conditional law of every future wealth increment given F t depends on the past only through (G t , S t , q t-); conditioning a strategy on the level, or on any other adapted quantity, adds no information about future rewards, so the control problem lives on the state (G, S, q). Time: the model is time-homogeneous and (2.17) an ergodic average, so the optimum is sought among stationary state policies, the standard reduction for ergodic criteria and part of what the verification theory below delivers on the surrogate. Symmetry: Definition 2.2 is invariant under (G, ↑) → (-G, ↓) and (2.16) under exchanging buys with sells, so every policy has a mirror image with the same rate, and a symmetric optimum exists. We therefore look for the optimum of (2.17) among symmetric threshold strategies: for a band half-width θ > 0, +1, G t ≤ -θ (buy: the mid is cheap), -1, G t ≥ +θ (sell: the mid is dear), q θ t-, otherwise (hold, no churn).

(3.1) Read (3.1) as a target position, not an order: when G t touches -θ or +θ the order sent is the difference q θ t -q θ t-, one lot at the first entry and two lots at every fill thereafter, flipping the position through zero without ever resting there.

The class is not an ansatz. Match each sold lot to the earliest not-yetmatched bought lot, and each buy-to-cover to the earliest unmatched short sale: this pairs the executed lots into round trips (one lot bought and one lot sold: a position opened and later closed, in either order), leaving at most one lot unpaired, the position still open at T . Let n T be the number of round trips completed by time T ; for the i-th, let τ b i and τ s i be the fill times of its buy and sell legs, and write for the gap and , ϕ s i = ϕ τ s i for the half-spread at each leg. Summing the trade bookings of (2.16), the wealth of every three-valued strategy, the class to which Proposition 2.2 reduces the problem, decomposes as term by term, in the order displayed: one summand per completed round trip, worth the traverse of the gap minus both half-spreads whether the trip is long or short; a zero-mean martingale, the bounded position integrated against the martingale X; and a remainder, the still-open trip marked to market: at most one lot times a gap of bounded mean (P2), an O(1) that vanishes against T . Take expectations in (3.2) and divide by T : the martingale has mean zero, the remainder vanishes against T , and only the trips survive,

The long-run rate is trips per unit time, times what a trip pays. A strategy therefore earns only through where it places its two legs, and we look for the optimum among threshold rules: trade when the gap clears a threshold, one per side; the depth itself is the object of the optimisation, since a deeper band earns more per trip but waits longer between trips. How far can the restriction to the band be trusted? The answer differs between the paper's two levels, and it should be kept straight. Proposition 2.2 is exact and pathwise; its layer argument reads verbatim on the surrogate, so "all admissible strategies" below includes fractional inventories. The step from all admissible strategies down to the flip band is different: it is a theorem only on the Gaussian surrogate introduced below (3.4), assembled from the literature in three pieces. Thresholds: for a mean-reverting diffusion under proportional costs, optimal entry and exit are first-passage thresholds, over all admissible strategies, time-varying and level-dependent ones included; the verification proofs are [36] for a positive mean-reverting asset, [35] for general one-dimensional diffusions, and [26] for the OU asset with a complete analysis. The criterion: those theorems discount; the long-run average of (2.17) is the renewal-reward evaluation of the trading cycle, as in [9], with ergodic verification along the vanishing-discount lines of [4]. Symmetry and no flat zone: mirror invariance forces the symmetric band, and Appendix A.8 rules out resting flat between the legs. On the exact jump process the same reduction is a conjecture supported by the same structure (Markov state, ergodic criterion, monotone trip payoff, mirror symmetry): a verification theorem for the parity-locked jump process is open, and the simulations of Section 3.1 test the surrogate's timing within the band class, not the optimality of the class.

The thresholds can also be taken parity-blind: the refinement θ(S) moves the rate by O(p), with p the open-book occupancy (2.9), the same order as the cost freeze below. Appendix A.8 also records the exact accounting: an excursion to flat is worth, in expectation, q(G a -G b ) -2ϕ relative to holding, and an instantaneous round trip pays the full spread for a traverse of zero. (A risk-averse criterion would reopen a flat zone around zero; we do not pursue it.) Hence (3.1), with a single number left to choose: θ. Proposition 3.1 prices the band exactly, carrying the half-spread ϕ F realised at each fill; one convention then lightens the optimisation. Fills in open books are the exception, the open state's occupancy being the p of (2.9); from (3.5) on we freeze the cost at its tight-book value, ϕ := δ/2, returning to what the freeze drops in Section 4. where π F is the stationary law of the post-fill chain, m(θ) the stationary expected time between opposite fills, and G F and ϕ F the gap and the half-spread at a fill, with θ ≤ E π F |G F | < θ + δ: the gap leaves (-θ, θ) either by diffusion, exactly at the edge, or by a jump, past it. Proof. The states of (G, S, q) observed at successive fills form a Markov chain; a diffusivecrossing construction gives it an accessible atom and a uniformly finite mean inter-fill time, hence positive Harris recurrence with invariant law π F , and m(θ) is the mean inter-fill time under π F . Each fill flips the inventory by two lots, each lot earning |G F | -ϕ F , so a cycle carries reward 4 E π F [|G F | -ϕ F ] and has mean length 2m(θ); the regenerative ratio gives (3.3). The two markings agree because W -W X = qG is bounded in L 1 , and on W X the inventory term q s-dX s is a zero-mean martingale. The bound on E π F |G F | is the maximal jump, δ. Every step is written out in Appendix A.7.

Everything so far is exact. Here exactness ends: m(θ) solves a coupled integro-differential system driven by the nonlocal generator of (G, S), and it has no closed form. We therefore evaluate the passage times on a surrogate (uniqueness: Appendix A.9). Let G be the unique Gaussian diffusion with the gap's exact conditional mean and covariance structure (2.13)-(2.14), and write m(θ) := E -θ [T +θ ], with T y := inf{t ≥ 0 : Gt = y}, for its passage time, in closed form an erfi (Appendix B). The object we maximise is the surrogate rate R(θ) = 2 (θ -ϕ) m(θ) . (3.5) Two distinct symbols are needed: m(θ) is a stationary mean over the fill chain of the true book, which begins each leg outside the band, at ∓|G F |, whereas m(θ) is the passage time of the surrogate from -θ to +θ. The construction of G assumes nothing: every parameter is an identity of the model, (2.13)-(2.14). Its use, however, is an approximation, and the three errors it introduces differ in status. (a) Replacing E π F |G F | by θ understates the reward, and the overshoot bound θ ≤ E π F |G F | < θ + δ of Proposition 3.1 makes that error of relative order δ/(θ -ϕ), rigorously: the denominator is the margin, not the threshold, and at the optimum (3.7) it equals u * δ/s G . (b) Replacing E π F [ϕ F ] by ϕ = δ/2 overstates the reward, by at most δ 2 π F (open) per lot, small by the occupancy of open books (Section 4) and pulling against (a). (c) Replacing m(θ) by m(θ) replaces the timing, and here the moments carry us no further: a first-passage time is not a function of the conditional mean and stationary covariance, so matching those two moments does not by itself control m(θ) -m(θ). What we invoke instead is the diffusion approximation of the limit theorems for microstructure point processes [8] (the same idealisation by which Avellaneda and Stoikov model the mid as a Brownian motion [6]), under which, in the regime where a fill is preceded by many small jumps, the timing error too is expected to be of relative order δ/θ. (c) is a heuristic, not a theorem: a proof that | m(θ) -m(θ)|/m(θ) = O(δ/θ) is left open, and the optimal rate (3.8) below is exact only for the surrogate. This is where we work: δ ≪ θ -ϕ, which forces δ ≪ θ.

The band equation. One fact about mean reversion finishes the problem. For thresholds beyond about one standard deviation, the surrogate's waiting time obeys Kramers' law [25]: maximum (Lemma B.1).) Patience is paid from the tails of the gap: hold out for a wider traverse when the gap disperses more, settle for less when the spread forces the band deep. Zero for the impatient. At θ = ϕ each round trip nets exactly zero while taking positive time, so R(ϕ) = 0: the myopic rule (trade as soon as the gap covers the spread) earns nothing. The optimal band exceeds break-even by θ * -ϕ = s 2 G /θ * , and every unit of profit is the option value of waiting for a deeper reversion. (In the exact model the impatient rule keeps only the overshoot income net of the occasional open-book cost, E π F [|G F | -ϕ F ] ∈ (-δ/2, δ) per lot: the zero is the δ/s G → 0 limit of that income.)

p.s: The surrogate optimum, tested against the exact model
p.t: One approximation stands between the formula and the model: the surrogate of (3.4), whose timing error was left heuristic. We test it where it matters: at the optimum. Simulating the exact jump model of Definitions 2.1-2.2 and sweeping the band around the surrogate optimum θ D of Appendix B, Figure 4 reads off the realised rate and its true maximiser. The sweep is over the band class: it tests where the surrogate places the optimum and the rate it assigns there, not the optimality of thresholds themselves, which Section 3 left as a conjecture on the exact process. Two things come out, and both were expected. (a) The exact rate tracks the surrogate over the whole band, and its true maximiser sits a little inside θ D : by around a fifth across the swept range of γ, edging up as the band widens. A jump carries the gap past the threshold, so the reward arrives at a width slightly short of the one the continuous surrogate would pick. (b) The cost of this misplacement is small precisely because the rate is flat at its top (Lemma B.1): over the sweep, setting the band at θ D rather than at the exact peak forfeits three to four percent of rate, and setting it at the band-equation root θ * , which sits outside θ D at these γ, five to six. The heuristic step above is thus confirmed where it is used: the surrogate misplaces the optimum by a controlled amount and misprices it by less. In practice the flatness cuts the other way too: essentially all of the loss is recovered anywhere in [0.8, 0.9] θ D . A practitioner may nudge the band slightly inward, but either

The band at work. Figure 5 closes the section on one sample path of the exact model: the fills, the flips, the thresholds breathing with the spread, and the wealth growing at the optimal rate.

The myopic rule, trade as soon as the gap covers the spread, breaks even on the surrogate by construction; whatever a strategy earns, it earns by declining trades that rule would take. One number governs everything. In the gap's own units, s G for threshold and margin, αs G for rate, the market enters through one number: γ = ϕ/s G , the half-spread over the typical gap. Two assets with the same γ share the same band. When the gap barely exceeds the spread (γ large), the band sits deep and the rate is exponentially small; when dispersion dominates (γ small), the band-equation root tightens toward one standard deviation, while the exact optimum drops inside it below γ ≈ 0.28 (Section 3). Gaps are wide, and the band with them, when the fundamental is noisy or the book corrects lazily: )/2α exactly, by (2.14), with σ 2 M a stationary mean that Remark 2.1 brackets. The optimum is forgiving. Because the optimum is an interior maximum of a smooth curve, an error ε in the threshold costs only O(ε 2 ) in rate (Figure 3, right). The strategy does not require knowing α and s G precisely, a practical virtue, since both must be estimated. Where the cost is paid. The spread is wide only while the book is open, and in the model of Definition 2.2 open books are transitional by construction: entered by the open moves and left by the closes; their occupancy is the p of (2.9), small in liquid large-tick books [14]. The band's fills therefore occur, as a rule, in tight books at ϕ = δ/2, and freezing the cost there, as Section 3 does, misprices only the fills that land in open books: exactly

What we left out. (a) The gap is not directly observable: X is latent, and a trading version of this paper must filter it from quotes and trades. The ingredients for that attack are on the shelf. The model of Section 2.3 is a state-space system: a Brownian state observed through a point process whose intensities are linear in the state. The implied filter is the point-process one [16], and both channels of the observation inform the latent state. A jump of M reweights the posterior on the gap by the intensity of the observed move and shifts it by the move's known size. A quiet spell reweights it toward small gaps, because the total event rate grows with dislocation. The estimate of X is therefore a function of the movement, and of the non-movement, of M . Kalman recursions apply at the surrogate level, where the counting observation aggregates to a Gaussian one. Likelihood estimation for order flow driven by a latent Brownian price, the structure here, is developed in [15]; and the efficient price is recovered from tick data under uncertainty zones in [32]. Estimation costs performance relative to the full-information benchmark solved here; how much is a filtering question we leave open. The parameters are the second estimation problem: baselines and loadings are identified by standard point-process likelihood [13], as in [31], while the reduced pair (α, s G ) needs no book-level data at all: α is the decay rate of the gap's autocovariance (2.14), σ X is delivered by two-scale realised variance [37], and Hasbrouck's decomposition recovers the permanent component from trades and quotes [21]. (b) Beyond estimation: liquidity providers may respond strategically to being picked off at the gap's extremes, which turns the problem into a game. (c) The switching problem can be attacked on the point process of Section 2.3 itself, replacing the surrogate passage times of (3.4) by the exact ones, with overshoot then a feature, not an error term. (d) The objective (2.17) is an expectation, not a utility, a modelling choice. A concave utility, or the Sharpe variant that [9] solves for the OU asset, would price the variance of the always-full position, and the optimum changes shape: a flat zone reopens around zero, interior positions can become optimal (Proposition 2.2), and the optimal thresholds themselves move. Each of these is a natural continuation; all start from the frame built here.

Building the book from the bid shows that the spread merely duplicates the parity of the mid (the parity lock), so the gap is the only continuous state variable. In a mutually exciting book the gap's reversion at the book's leaning rate α is a theorem, and the fundamental is proved to be the long-run forecast of the mid. With waiting times evaluated on the exactly matched Gaussian surrogate, the optimal trading of that reversion is a one-dimensional switching problem with a closed-form answer: a symmetric no-churn band with θ * (θ * -ϕ) = s 2 G and rate αs G 2/π e -u * 2 /2 . Trading as soon as the gap covers the spread earns exactly zero. The result is meant in the spirit of Avellaneda and Stoikov [6]: a stylised model, an explicit solution, and formulas simple enough to reason with. Three assumptions carry the result: (a) the balanced response (2.8), whose bite is bounded by the open-book occupancy in (2.10); (b) the small trader, whose orders leave the intensities (2.5) unmoved; and (c) the observability of the gap. Two questions remain open on the jump process itself: the timing error of the surrogate, whose order δ/θ is left heuristic, and the optimality of the band class, stated here as a conjecture. Section 4 sketches the corresponding continuations: estimation, the provider's game, the switching problem attacked on the jump process directly, and the risk-adjusted criterion.

A process satisfying Definitions 2.1-2.2 exists and is nonexplosive. Conditionally on the path of X, the intensities (2.5) are continuous, locally bounded functions of time between events, so the book is built by iterating Ogata thinning from one event to the next [13]. Explosion is excluded by the drift bound proved in A.4: with τ n the n-th event and V = G 2 , the bound LV ≤ -αV + d ≤ d gives, by Dynkin's formula with the standard double localisation and Fatou, E[V (G t∧τn )] ≤ V (G 0 ) + d t uniformly in n; since the total intensity is affine, m λ m ≤ c0 + c1 |G|, it follows that uniformly in n: the expected number of events up to any fixed time is finite, and τ n → ∞ almost surely. (P1) Itô for a jump process minus a Brownian motion. Let G = M -X with M of finite activity and pure jump and X continuous. Then [G] t = σ 2 X t + u≤t (∆M u ) 2 : X contributes its quadratic variation, M its jumps, and the cross term vanishes because X is continuous. Consequently (P2) Foster-Lyapunov. Let a Markov process have extended generator L, and suppose there exist V ≥ 0 with compact sublevel sets and constants c, d > 0 such that LV ≤ -cV + d, and that all compact sets are petite. Then the process is positive Harris recurrent, has a unique invariant law π, and π(V ) ≤ d/c [28]. For (G, S) the petiteness is supplied by the noise the model already carries: σ X > 0 gives the gap a nondegenerate Brownian component between events, and the positive baselines let the parity flip anywhere: from any initial state, over a unit window, the event "exactly k ∈ {0, 1} book events, with the Brownian increment in a prescribed interval" has probability bounded below, locally uniformly in the initial state, and lands (G, S) in any given open set with positive probability. The process is therefore ψ-irreducible and a T -process in the sense of [28], for which all compact sets are petite.

If visits to an accessible atom split the path into i.i.d. cycles of finite mean length, with rewards of bounded size and finite expected number per cycle, then T -1 E[ τ k ≤T R k ] → E[reward per cycle]/E[cycle length], almost surely and in the mean [5, Ch. VI]; equivalently, the ratio of stationary means over the embedded chain.

p.s: A.2 Proof of Fact 1 (the parity lock)
p.t: Proof. Measure the mid in half-ticks: k t := 2M t /δ = 2B t /δ + S t /δ. The bid lives on the tick grid, so 2B t /δ is an even integer and the parity of k t is that of S t /δ, for any spread on the grid: an odd spread makes k t odd, an even one makes it even, which is (2.3). Within (2.2) only δ and 2δ are available, so the map inverts: S t = δ iff k t is odd and S t = 2δ iff k t is even. The correspondence holds at t = 0 by construction and is preserved by every move of (2.7): a slide changes k by ±2 and leaves the spread; an open changes k by ±1 and takes the spread from δ to 2δ; a close is its mirror image. In each of the six moves the parity of k and the value of S change together, so the lock holds for all t: the spread is a deterministic function of the mid, and (G, S) is a Markov process in the single continuous coordinate G together with a parity bit. No dynamics for S needs to be specified: it is read off M .

p.s: A.5 A lemma on the two markings
p.t: Lemma A. 1. Under (2.16), W t -W X t = q t G t for all t; in particular sup t E |W t -W X t | < ∞, and the two markings define the same long-run rate. Proof. Step 1 (the difference is an exact differential). By (2.16), dW t -dW X t = q t-dM t -dX t + G t dq t = q t-dG t + G t dq t . Since q is piecewise constant and of finite variation while G is a semimartingale, integration by parts gives d(qG) t = q t-dG t + G t-dq t + d[q, G] t with [q, G] t = s≤t ∆q s ∆G s , and G t-∆q t + ∆q t ∆G t = G t ∆q t . Hence dW t -dW X t = d(q t G t ) and, starting flat, W t -W X t = q t G t . The identity requires the trade term in dW X to carry the post-jump gap G t dq t , not G t-dq t , the execution convention of the model; with G t-the identity would carry the extra term ∆q ∆G. Step 2 (boundedness). |q| ≤ 1 and sup t E|G t | < ∞ by the drift bound in Step 4 of A.4, so E|W t -W X t | is bounded uniformly in t and the two markings define the same long-run rate.

p.t: The family is jointly measurable, and integrable uniformly in u: the gains are dominated by δ times the number of book events, of finite mean by (P0), and the costs by δ times twice the number of trades of q, of finite mean by admissibility. Fubini then gives E[W T (q)] = 1 0 E[W T (a u )] du ≤ sup u E[W T (a u )] for every T : an average cannot beat its best layer.

One inequality in (2.19) is inclusion: a three-valued strategy is an admissible interval-valued one. For the other, enlarge the filtration by a draw U , uniform on (0, 1], taken at time zero independently of the book (the independence leaves every intensity and every martingale statement unchanged, and admissibility is understood throughout to permit such a draw), and set â := a U , a single admissible strategy with values in {-1, 0, +1}. By independence, Fubini and the integrability of Step 4, E[W T (â)] = 1 0 E[W T (a u )] du = E[W T (q)] for every T, so â and q share the whole function T → E[W T ], hence the same lower-limit rate, and (2.19) follows. Remark A.1. Randomisation is a convenience, not a loophole. On the market filtration alone, the moment bound of Appendix A.4 gives K := sup t≥0 E|G t | < ∞ and, by (2.12), T -1 E[W T (a u )] ≤ αK uniformly in T ≥ 1 and u; reverse Fatou applied to (2.18) then yields lim sup T T -1 E[W T (q)] ≤ sup u lim sup T T -1 E[W T (a u )]: no interval-valued strategy beats the three-valued value in the upper-limit sense either, and the optimal band attains its rate as a true limit (Appendix A.7). A.7 Proof of Proposition 3.1 Proof. Step 1 (the two markings agree). By (2.16) and Appendix A.5, W t -W X t = q t G t . Since |q| ≤ 1 and sup t E|G t | < ∞ (Step 4 of A.4 bounds E[G 2 t ] from any start), the difference is bounded in L 1 uniformly in t, so E[W T ]/T and E[W X T ]/T have the same limit. Step 2 (the inventory term vanishes). q t-is predictable and bounded and X is a square-integrable martingale, so T 0 q s-dX s is a martingale of zero mean. Hence E[W X T ] = E -T 0 G t dq t -T 0 ϕ t |dq t | : the rate depends on the strategy only through the state at its trades.

p.s: Step 3 (the mean time between fills is finite, uniformly).
p.t: Under the band (3.1) the inventory is ±1 after the first fill, and the fill times τ 1 < τ 2 < • • • are the successive times the gap reaches the far threshold; the post-fill gap satisfies |G τ k | ∈ [θ, θ + δ) by Step 7 below. Positive recurrence of the fill chain requires the mean time to leave a bounded region, an outward hitting, which Harris recurrence of (G, S) does not by itself deliver. It does here. Fix h > 0 and let Λ bound the total intensity m λ m on {|G| ≤ 2θ + 2δ}, finite because each intensity is affine in |G|. From any state with |G| ≤ θ + δ, consider the event A: no book event on [0, h], and the Brownian path stays in a tube that carries the gap monotonically enough across the far threshold within [0, h] while never leaving {|G| ≤ 2θ + 2δ}. Conditionally on any such Brownian path, the no-event probability is at least e -Λh , because until the first event the gap moves by the Brownian alone and the tube confines it where the intensities are bounded by Λ; and the tube itself has probability bounded below, uniformly over the compact set of starting points, by the standard tube estimate for Brownian motion. Hence P(fill within h) ≥ e -Λh p tube =: p > 0 uniformly, and by the strong Markov property P(τ k+1 -τ k > jh | F τ k ) ≤ (1-p) j , so E[τ k+1 -τ k | F τ k ] ≤ h/p uniformly over post-fill states.

p.s: Step 4 (an accessible atom, hence positive Harris).
p.t: By the strong Markov property of (G, S), the post-fill states (G τ k , S τ k , q τ k ) form a Markov chain on the compact set {θ ≤ |g| < θ + δ} × {δ, 2δ} × {±1}. On the event A of Step 3 the crossing is diffusive (no book event fires), so the arrival gap is exactly ±θ and the parity arrives frozen at its post-fill value; a variant of A with exactly one parity-flipping event early in the window (an open if the book is tight, total rate at least 2µ o on the tube; a close if open, at least 2µ c ) and no other events delivers the crossing with the opposite parity, the tube absorbing the δ/2 kick. Both variants have probability bounded below, uniformly over post-fill states. The chain therefore reaches each of the four states a = (±θ, σ, ∓1), σ ∈ {δ, 2δ}, in one step with probability at least ε > 0 from everywhere: these are accessible atoms. Visits to a fixed atom then split the path into i.i.d. cycles whose mean length is finite (a geometric number of fills, each of conditional mean at most h/p by Step 3), so the chain is positive Harris with an invariant law π F [5, Ch. VI]. Write m(θ) := E π F [τ k+1 -τ k ] ≤ h/p < ∞ for the stationary mean time between opposite fills; mirror symmetry makes it the same for both legs. This is the definition of m(θ) in (3.3); it is not the passage time of any diffusion.

At a sell fill the gap is G F ≥ θ, the half-spread is ϕ F ∈ {δ/2, δ} read off the parity at the fill, and the inventory flips from +1 to -1: dq = -2 and, by (2.16), the X-marked cash flow is -G F • (-2) -ϕ F • 2 = 2(G F -ϕ F ). A buy fill at -G ′ F gives 2(G ′ F -ϕ ′ F ). A cycle contains one of each, so its reward has mean 4 E π F [|G F |-ϕ F ] and its length mean 2m(θ).

Rewards per fill are bounded by 2(θ + δ) and cycles have finite mean length, so (P3), applied at the atom of Step 4, gives R(θ) = 4 E π F [|G F |ϕ F ] 2m(θ) , which is (3.3). The convergence is almost sure, so the pathwise rate equals this stationary ratio, the ergodic identity, and the lim inf in (2.17) is attained from any start.
The gap leaves (-θ, θ) either continuously, in which case |G F | = θ, or at a jump of M , whose size is at most δ by (2.7). Hence θ ≤ |G F | < θ + δ pathwise, and the same bounds hold under π F .

We record what is proved and what is cited. Let q be admissible and consider an excursion to flat: the trader holds q ∈ {-1, 1}, unwinds to 0 at a time ς a when the gap is G a , and re-enters the same q at ς b > ς a when the gap is G b .

By (2.16) the X-marked cash flows of the two trades are q G a -ϕ at ς a (where dq = -q) and -q G b -ϕ at ς b (where dq = +q). Between them the inventory is flat, so the only other term, q dX, vanishes pathwise. Holding through the interval adds only the inventory martingale q (X ς b -X ςa ), of zero mean at the stopping times. In expectation the excursion is therefore worth relative to holding, the half-spread being paid on each side (we write the frozen tight-book ϕ; carrying the realised ϕ F changes nothing in the comparison).

p.s: Step 2 (what Step 1 does and does not settle).
p.t: Two consequences are immediate: an instantaneous round trip (ς b = ς a ) pays 2ϕ for a traverse of zero and is never optimal, and the excursion is ex post profitable exactly when q(G a -G b ) > 2ϕ. What Step 1 does not settle is whether such an excursion can be chosen ex ante: the trader commits at one stopping time, the payoff depends on the gap at a later one, and a pathwise inequality about a realised swing is not a statement about conditional expectations. It does not by itself dominate holding.
